description: Our team combines creativity, communication, and technical skills to develop innovative solutions. We have strengths in website development, basic programming, and design. We value teamwork, creative thinking, and problem-solving. We are also interested in machine learning and its potential to create intelligent solutions. We are ready to collaborate, learn, and innovate at the NASA Challenge 2026.
summary:
Orbital Fix is a free pixel-art web game where anyone, from a curious student to a future engineer, plans and flies a real-style science mission in 3 to 5 minutes.

You start like a real mission team: choose a science goal (water ice on the Moon, Europa's ice shell, Titan's methane seas), then build a spacecraft from snap-together parts while balancing four real constraints: mass, power, data and budget. A cheap rocket can't lift a heavy ship, and the best parts never all fit the budget, so every choice is a trade-off. Then you fly it: launch inside the window, survive a solar storm, dodge debris, burn for orbit insertion, repair a broken unit the way astronauts do (tether, power isolation, star-pattern bolts) and send your science home through the Deep Space Network as the Earth turns.

Each storm is linked to today's real Sun through NASA's DONKI space-weather data, and every task ends with a short "In real life" fact. A 2-minute CubeSat tutorial teaches the basics first. It runs in any browser, in 4 languages, with mouse, keyboard or touch.
details:
WHAT IT IS

Orbital Fix is a browser game about the part of space exploration most people never see: designing a mission so it survives, and fixing it when something breaks. The challenge asked for a game that makes mission design understandable and fun. We turned it into one short loop (plan, build, fly, repair, send data home) that takes 3 to 5 minutes and can be replayed with different choices.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Science goal first. Every mission starts with a question, not a rocket: map future landing sites on the Moon, find water ice in dark craters, study Jupiter's auroras, measure how thick Europa's ice is, map Titan's methane seas. The goal decides which instrument is worth the most.

2. Build the spacecraft. Nine slots (power, battery, propulsion, computer, antenna, instrument, data storage, thermal, protection) snap together and the ship changes visibly as you add parts. Four meters (mass, power, data and budget) react to every choice. All ships are checked by our rules: every rocket on screen can launch at least one ship, and a "max everything" ship never fits the budget, so money is a real constraint. Unspent budget becomes reserve credits you can spend during the flight.

3. Launch window. Launch when the destination enters the green arc, like a real transfer window.

4. Cruise events. A solar storm (point the shield at the Sun and switch to safe mode before the particles arrive), space debris (plan avoidance burns) or an air leak (find it with an ultrasonic detector). Storms are tied to the real Sun: if NASA DONKI reports an active Sun today, a storm is certain.

5. Orbit insertion. Hold the engine burn only while the ship crosses the green arc, or waste fuel.

6. Repair. A unit breaks, as in real missions (inspired by ISS spacewalks and Hubble Servicing Mission 4): plan a safe tether path, isolate power on a circuit diagram without cutting life support, tighten bolts in a star pattern and install the new unit. Robotic missions add light-time delay: your commands arrive minutes later.

7. Send the science home. Keep a Deep Space Network dish (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) locked on the spacecraft as the Earth turns.

8. Report. A score across four pillars (design, science, operations and repair) and a short debrief of what you did well.

Six destinations (Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Europa, Saturn, Titan), crewed and robotic, each with real travel times, sunlight, radio delay and gravity. Historical presets let players fly a ship like LRO, Perseverance, Juno, Europa Clipper, Cassini or Huygens. A 2-minute CubeSat tutorial (build a 3U CubeSat under 4 kg, ride to orbit, deploy and downlink during a ground-station pass) is the first step for beginners.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Low barrier, real depth: little text, few numbers, short puzzles that teach by doing. Facts appear after each task as short "In real life" cards, never as walls of text.

- It teaches trade-offs, not trivia: why mass, power, data and money fight each other, why launch windows exist, why repairs follow strict procedures, why radio delay matters.

- Real data, honestly labelled: NASA DONKI space weather (with NOAA GOES flares as a labelled fallback) shows the real Sun of the day, and the game says so plainly when the service is down.

- Accessible: 4 languages (English, Portuguese, Spanish, Hindi), mouse, keyboard and touch on every puzzle, three difficulty levels (Cadet, Engineer, Flight Director), reduced-motion support, status shown by shape as well as colour, and local team mode for classrooms (1 to 4 players with mission roles).

- Free, no install, no login: it opens in any browser at orbitalfix.wiki.

HOW WE BUILT IT

- TypeScript, React 19, TanStack Start, Vite and Tailwind CSS; Framer Motion for animation; hosted on Vercel.

- All game rules (economy, events, repairs, orbit insertion, downlink, scoring, CubeSat) are pure, deterministic modules with automated tests (142 tests). One test enumerates every possible spacecraft (about 39,000 combinations) to guarantee that no beginner choice is a dead end.

- Sound effects are synthesized in the browser (Web Audio), with no audio files.

- Pixel art and short video loops were generated with Google Flow and processed by our own scripts (background removal, colour correction so planets keep their real colours). They are labelled "AI-generated" inside the game.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We tested with players and ran a 50-question questionnaire with the team. Testers found the first version confusing, so we added a tutorial, a briefing card before each task, larger text and a radio CapCom who guides every phase. Testers also found an affordable rocket that could never launch, so we rebuilt the economy and verified it against every possible ship. The mission was kept short (3 to 5 minutes) so it fits a class period, and failure never ends the game instantly: you redo the step with a penalty and learn why it failed.
